records.edition: Long translation (1862)
records.bibliographic_citation: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations II.1, trans. George Long (1862).
records.display_summary: Marcus frames difficult encounters within a Stoic claim that human beings are naturally social and should resist hatred even when others behave badly.

records.edition: Long translation (1862)
records.bibliographic_citation: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VI.6, trans. George Long (1862).
records.display_summary: A compact Stoic instruction to preserve one's own character rather than imitate wrongdoing in retaliation.

records.edition: Long translation (1862)
records.bibliographic_citation: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VIII.47, trans. George Long (1862).
records.display_summary: Marcus distinguishes an external event from the evaluative judgment that can intensify distress, while emphasizing that judgments can be reconsidered.

records.edition: George Bell and Sons, 1890
records.bibliographic_citation: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1, trans. George Long, in The Discourses of Epictetus, with the Encheiridion and Fragments (London: George Bell and Sons, 1890).
records.display_summary: Epictetus opens the Enchiridion by separating one's own judgments, impulses, desires, and aversions from externals such as property, reputation, office, and the body.

records.edition: George Bell and Sons, 1890
records.bibliographic_citation: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5, trans. George Long (1890).
records.display_summary: Epictetus argues that evaluative opinions shape distress and urges examination of those opinions rather than automatic blame.

records.edition: George Bell and Sons, 1890
records.bibliographic_citation: Epictetus, Enchiridion 8, trans. George Long (1890).
records.display_summary: Epictetus counsels reducing distress created by demanding that reality conform to preference.

records.edition: Loeb Classical Library, Vol. I
records.bibliographic_citation: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 13.4, trans. Richard M. Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, 1917).
records.display_summary: In Letter 13 Seneca distinguishes actual adversity from fear generated in advance by imagining what may happen.

records.edition: Loeb Classical Library, Vol. I
records.bibliographic_citation: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 63.4, trans. Richard M. Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, 1917).
records.display_summary: Seneca allows grief and tears while encouraging remembrance to become capable of containing affection as well as pain.

records.edition: Loeb Classical Library, Vol. I
records.bibliographic_citation: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 47.11, trans. Richard M. Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, 1917).
records.display_summary: In a letter criticizing Roman treatment of enslaved people, Seneca argues for reciprocal humane treatment across social rank.

records.edition: Loeb Classical Library, Vol. II
records.bibliographic_citation: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 78.20, trans. Richard M. Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, 1920).
records.display_summary: Seneca addresses illness by distinguishing bodily limitation from remaining possibilities for reflection, learning, and character.

records.edition: George Bell and Sons public-domain translation
records.bibliographic_citation: Seneca, De Ira II.29, trans. Aubrey Stewart, public-domain George Bell and Sons edition.
records.display_summary: Seneca recommends delaying angry action so judgment can recover before response.

records.edition: Moral Essays, Loeb Classical Library
records.bibliographic_citation: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 1, trans. John W. Basore, Moral Essays, Loeb Classical Library (1932).
records.display_summary: Seneca argues that the felt shortness of life is often connected to how attention and time are spent rather than duration alone.

records.edition: Loeb Classical Library, Vol. I
records.bibliographic_citation: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 28.1, trans. Richard M. Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, 1917).
records.display_summary: Seneca argues that travel alone cannot resolve distress that one carries internally.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; teaching attributed to the Buddha

records.bibliographic_citation: Dhammapada 160, trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 10.1 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1881).

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; teaching attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. X, Part I (1881)
records.bibliographic_citation: Dhammapada 204, trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 10.1 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1881).
records.display_summary: The verse ranks health, contentment, trustworthy relationship, and liberation as forms of well-being beyond material accumulation alone.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; teaching attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. X, Part I (1881)
records.bibliographic_citation: Dhammapada 277, trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 10.1 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1881).
records.display_summary: This is Müller's compact rendering of the Buddhist teaching that conditioned formations are impermanent.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; teaching attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. X, Part II (1881)
records.bibliographic_citation: Sutta-Nipata 1.8, v. 144, trans. Viggo Fausböll, Sacred Books of the East 10.2 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1881).
records.display_summary: The Mettasutta develops impartial goodwill toward living beings without making that goodwill dependent on social closeness.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; teaching attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. X, Part II (1881)
records.bibliographic_citation: Sutta-Nipata 1.8, v. 147, trans. Viggo Fausböll, Sacred Books of the East 10.2 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1881).
records.display_summary: The verse places non-deception and non-contempt inside a broader practice of goodwill, including when anger or resentment is present.

records.edition: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. X, Part II (1881)
records.bibliographic_citation: Sutta-Nipata 1.3, trans. Viggo Fausböll, Sacred Books of the East 10.2 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1881).
records.display_summary: The Rhinoceros discourse repeatedly praises solitary renunciant practice and freedom from entangling attachments.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; discourse attributed to the Buddha
records.book_chapter_section: MN 21, Kakacupama Sutta; early instruction section
records.edition: Further Dialogues of the Buddha, Vol. I (1926)
records.bibliographic_citation: Majjhima Nikaya 21, trans. Lord Chalmers, Further Dialogues of the Buddha, Vol. I (London: Humphrey Milford/Oxford University Press, 1926).
records.display_summary: Early in MN 21, before the discourse's later extreme simile, the teaching recommends maintaining compassion and avoiding hostile speech when hearing criticism.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; discourse attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: Further Dialogues of the Buddha, Vol. I (1926)
records.bibliographic_citation: Majjhima Nikaya 4, trans. Lord Chalmers, Further Dialogues of the Buddha, Vol. I (1926).
records.display_summary: The discourse explicitly acknowledges that solitude can evoke fear and dread, then frames disciplined conduct and attention as part of meeting that fear.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; discourse attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: Further Dialogues of the Buddha, Vol. I (1926)
records.bibliographic_citation: Majjhima Nikaya 63, trans. Lord Chalmers, Further Dialogues of the Buddha, Vol. I (1926).
records.display_summary: The discourse declines to settle a set of speculative cosmological questions and redirects attention toward teachings presented as relevant to suffering and its cessation.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; discourse attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: Luzac & Company, 1902
records.bibliographic_citation: Udana 1.10, trans. D. M. Strong, The Udana; or, The Solemn Utterances of the Buddha (London: Luzac & Co., 1902).
records.display_summary: The Bahiya instruction trains attention to seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing without adding further identification or elaboration.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; teaching attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: Columbia University Indo-Iranian Series, Vol. V (1908)
records.bibliographic_citation: Itivuttaka 50, in Sayings of Buddha: The Iti-Vuttaka, trans. Justin Hartley Moore (New York: Columbia University Press, 1908).
records.display_summary: Itivuttaka 50 identifies greed, hatred, and delusion as three harmful roots, providing a compact early-Buddhist frame for reactive grasping and hostility.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Traditional Pali Canon; discourse attributed to the Buddha
records.edition: The Book of the Kindred Sayings, Vol. IV
records.bibliographic_citation: Samyutta Nikaya 36.9, trans. F. L. Woodward, The Book of the Kindred Sayings, Vol. IV, Pali Text Society.
records.display_summary: SN 36.9 describes pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings as conditioned and subject to change and cessation.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Laozi (traditional attribution); received text is composite
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Daodejing 8, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891).
records.display_summary: Chapter 8 develops water as an image for benefiting without contentious striving, accepting low places, and acting with situational timing.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Laozi (traditional attribution); received text is composite
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Daodejing 33, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: The chapter contrasts knowledge and power over others with self-knowledge and self-mastery, then turns to contentment and endurance.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Laozi (traditional attribution); received text is composite
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Daodejing 46, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: Chapter 46 contrasts unbounded wanting with contentment and presents 'enough' as a different measure of sufficiency.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Laozi (traditional attribution); received text is composite
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Daodejing 64, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: The surrounding chapter emphasizes addressing beginnings before disorder compounds and treating large developments as arising from small starts.

records.book_chapter_section: Inner Chapter 3, Nourishing the Lord of Life, §1
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Zhuangzi, Inner Chapter 3.1, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: The opening warns against exhausting finite life by trying to pursue limitless knowledge, before moving into a broader discussion of sustaining life.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Laozi (traditional attribution); received text is composite
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Daodejing 22, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: Chapter 22 links fewer desires, less self-display, less self-assertion, and less self-boasting with a form of non-contentious completeness.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Laozi (traditional attribution); received text is composite
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Daodejing 48, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: Chapter 48 contrasts accumulating learning with a Dao-oriented process of diminishing deliberate doing until action is no longer forced toward an ulterior end.

records.author_or_attributed_figure: Laozi (traditional attribution); received text is composite
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Daodejing 76, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: Chapter 76 contrasts the supple and flexible with the rigid and force-dependent, using living bodies and plants as its imagery.

records.book_chapter_section: Inner Chapter 1, Enjoyment in Untroubled Ease
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Zhuangzi, Inner Chapter 1, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: The chapter culminates in an ideal that is not anchored in self-fixation, accumulated merit, or fame, within a larger argument about dependence and untroubled wandering.

records.book_chapter_section: Inner Chapter 2, Adjustment of Controversies; butterfly dream passage
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Zhuangzi, Inner Chapter 2, butterfly-dream passage, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, SBE 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: The butterfly-dream passage destabilizes rigid confidence about perspective and identity and concludes by naming a 'transformation of things.'

records.book_chapter_section: Inner Chapter 4, Man in the World; useless-tree passages
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Zhuangzi, Inner Chapter 4, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: The chapter repeatedly uses trees judged useless by ordinary standards to question whether conventional utility exhausts a thing's value or determines whether it can flourish.

records.book_chapter_section: Inner Chapter 4, 'fasting of the mind' passage
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
records.bibliographic_citation: Zhuangzi, Inner Chapter 4, 'fasting of the mind' passage, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part I, SBE 39 (1891).
records.display_summary: The 'fasting of the mind' passage uses a dialogue about loosening preoccupation and fixed mental occupation before entering a difficult social situation.

records.school_or_lineage: Zhuangzi Outer Chapter 20; later authorship layer
records.author_or_attributed_figure: Zhuangzi received textual tradition; Outer Chapter, not securely historical Zhuang Zhou
records.book_chapter_section: Outer Chapter 20, Mountain Tree; empty-boat passage

records.bibliographic_citation: Zhuangzi, Outer Chapter 20, empty-boat passage, trans. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Part II, Sacred Books of the East 40 (1891).
records.display_summary: The empty-boat story contrasts a collision that provokes little anger when no agent is perceived with escalating anger when intention is attributed to another person.

records.bibliographic_citation: Bhagavad Gita. Translated by Sir Edwin Arnold as The Song Celestial. 1885. Project Gutenberg eBook #2388.

records.edition: The Song Celestial, 1885; Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
records.bibliographic_citation: Bhagavad Gita. Translated by Sir Edwin Arnold as The Song Celestial. 1885. Project Gutenberg eBook #2388.
records.display_summary: The text repeatedly treats steadiness amid gain/loss, pleasure/pain, and changing conditions as a discipline of action rather than emotional numbness.

records.edition: The Song Celestial, 1885; Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
records.bibliographic_citation: Bhagavad Gita. Translated by Sir Edwin Arnold as The Song Celestial. 1885. Project Gutenberg eBook #2388.
records.display_summary: The Gita describes how fixation, craving, and reactive desire can narrow judgment, while disciplined attention can interrupt that chain.

records.edition: The Song Celestial, 1885; Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
records.bibliographic_citation: Bhagavad Gita. Translated by Sir Edwin Arnold as The Song Celestial. 1885. Project Gutenberg eBook #2388.
records.display_summary: Arjuna's grief and fear are addressed within a metaphysical framework that distinguishes changing embodied life from the enduring principle described by the text.

records.school_or_lineage: Principal Upanishads; pre-systematic Vedanta source literature
records.edition: Sacred Books of the East, Vols. 1 and 15
records.bibliographic_citation: The Upanishads. Translated by F. Max Müller. Sacred Books of the East, Vols. 1 and 15. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1879-1884.

records.edition: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man

records.edition: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man
records.bibliographic_citation: Patanjali. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man. Interpretation by Charles Johnston. 1912.
records.display_summary: The Yoga Sutras analyze attachment, aversion, misidentification, and fear as recurring afflictive patterns that can condition action and attention.

records.edition: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man
records.bibliographic_citation: Patanjali. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man. Interpretation by Charles Johnston. 1912.
records.display_summary: The cultivation of friendliness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity is presented as a way of steadying the mind in relation to other people.

records.edition: The Chinese Classics / Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
records.bibliographic_citation: Confucius. Analects. Translated by James Legge. Public-domain electronic editions via Project Gutenberg.
records.display_summary: The Analects emphasizes learning, repeated practice, correction, and cultivation of character over defining a person by a single failure or fixed trait.

records.edition: The Chinese Classics / Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
records.bibliographic_citation: Confucius. Analects. Translated by James Legge. Public-domain electronic editions via Project Gutenberg.
records.display_summary: Confucian reciprocity asks a person to consider others while maintaining standards of conduct; relationship quality is tied to humane and appropriate action.

records.edition: The Chinese Classics / Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
records.bibliographic_citation: Confucius. Analects. Translated by James Legge. Public-domain electronic editions via Project Gutenberg.
records.display_summary: The Analects treats recognizing and correcting one's faults as part of cultivation, separating moral growth from permanent self-condemnation.

records.edition: The Chinese Classics / Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
records.bibliographic_citation: Confucius. Analects. Translated by James Legge. Public-domain electronic editions via Project Gutenberg.
records.display_summary: Learning is framed as a lifelong practice shaped by purpose, relationships, and conduct rather than a race toward immediate status.

records.edition: The Chinese Classics / public-domain collected edition
records.bibliographic_citation: Mencius. Mencius. Historical English translations by James Legge; contextual verification with Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Mencius'.
records.display_summary: Mencian ethics treats compassion and other moral dispositions as capacities that can be cultivated rather than proof that a person is irredeemably good or bad.

records.bibliographic_citation: Mencius. Mencius. Historical English translations by James Legge; contextual verification with Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Mencius'.

records.edition: The Chinese Classics / public-domain collected edition
records.bibliographic_citation: Mencius. Mencius. Historical English translations by James Legge; contextual verification with Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Mencius'.
records.display_summary: Mencian texts sometimes interpret hardship as a context in which capacities are tested and developed, while not treating suffering itself as inherently good.

records.edition: The Chinese Classics, Volume 1; Project Gutenberg eBook #3100
records.bibliographic_citation: The Great Learning and The Doctrine of the Mean. In The Chinese Classics, translated by James Legge. Project Gutenberg eBook #3100.
records.display_summary: The Great Learning links personal cultivation with relationships and wider responsibilities, emphasizing ordered attention from the self outward.

records.edition: The Chinese Classics, Volume 1; Project Gutenberg eBook #3100
records.bibliographic_citation: The Great Learning and The Doctrine of the Mean. In The Chinese Classics, translated by James Legge. Project Gutenberg eBook #3100.

records.edition: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, substantive revision 2024
records.bibliographic_citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. 'Japanese Zen Buddhist Philosophy.' Substantive revision 2024.

records.edition: 1934 English translation
records.bibliographic_citation: Wumen Huikai. The Gateless Gate. Historical translation by Nyogen Senzaki, 1934; contextual review via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Japanese Zen Buddhist Philosophy'.
records.display_summary: Koan literature deliberately frustrates ordinary conceptual habits; its role is practice within a tradition, not giving literal factual answers to existential or identity questions.

records.edition: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
records.bibliographic_citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. 'Jaina Philosophy.' First published 2023.
records.display_summary: Jaina ethics places non-harming, careful conduct, and self-mastery at the center of how one relates to other living beings.

records.edition: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
records.bibliographic_citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. 'Jaina Philosophy.' First published 2023.
records.display_summary: Jaina many-sidedness holds that a single description can capture only part of a complex reality, encouraging disciplined perspective-taking without saying every view is equally true.

records.edition: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
records.bibliographic_citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. 'Jaina Philosophy.' First published 2023.
records.display_summary: Non-attachment in Jaina ethics concerns reducing possessiveness and passions as part of a demanding ethical path.

records.edition: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
records.bibliographic_citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. 'Jaina Philosophy.' First published 2023.
records.display_summary: Jaina analyses of passion and attachment can be used as a philosophical lens on urges, provided they are not substituted for evidence-based care or medical support.

records.edition: G. Bell and Sons reprint, 1915; Project Gutenberg eBook #57342

records.edition: G. Bell and Sons reprint, 1915; Project Gutenberg eBook #57342
records.bibliographic_citation: Diogenes Laertius. Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers, Book X. Translated by C. D. Yonge. 1915 reprint; Project Gutenberg eBook #57342.
records.display_summary: Epicurean ethics gives friendship a central place in secure and pleasant living, making relationships part of flourishing rather than mere status.

records.edition: G. Bell and Sons reprint, 1915; Project Gutenberg eBook #57342
records.bibliographic_citation: Diogenes Laertius. Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers, Book X. Translated by C. D. Yonge. 1915 reprint; Project Gutenberg eBook #57342.
records.display_summary: Epicurean arguments aim to reduce fear of death by examining what death can mean for the one who dies, shifting attention toward living well in the present.

records.edition: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
records.bibliographic_citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. 'Ancient Ethical Theory.'
records.display_summary: Aristotelian ethics understands character as formed through repeated activity and practical judgment, allowing mistakes to be treated as part of cultivation rather than a permanent identity.

records.edition: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
records.bibliographic_citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. 'Ancient Ethical Theory.'
records.display_summary: Ancient Greek ethical theories ask what kind of life is worth living and how choices, relationships, and character contribute to flourishing.

records.edition: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man
records.bibliographic_citation: Patanjali. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man. Interpretation by Charles Johnston. 1912.
records.display_summary: Attachment and aversion can keep attention bound to a painful relational event; practice can notice those reactions without making them the whole identity.

records.edition: The Song Celestial, 1885; Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
records.bibliographic_citation: Bhagavad Gita. Translated by Sir Edwin Arnold as The Song Celestial. 1885. Project Gutenberg eBook #2388.
